lesson.title: Who's Driving? Internal and External Locus of Control
lesson.summary: Locus of control describes whether a person generally believes that what happens to them is caused mainly by their own actions, an internal locus, or by outside forces like luck, fate, or powerful others, an external locus, a concept developed by psychologist Julian Rotter.
lesson.body:
Attribution theory is usually applied one event at a time: why did this particular thing happen? Julian Rotter took a related idea and turned it into a stable personality dimension in 1966, asking a broader question: across your life in general, do you tend to believe that outcomes are caused by your own behavior and choices, or by forces outside your control? People who lean toward the first answer are said to have an internal locus of control, and tend to explain outcomes with statements like "I got the job because I prepared well." People who lean toward the second answer are said to have an external locus of control, and tend to explain the same kind of outcome with statements like "I got the job because the interviewer happened to like me" or "it was just luck."

Locus of control is often confused with a related but distinct idea, self-efficacy, which is Albert Bandura's term for how confident someone feels in their own ability to successfully carry out a specific task or behavior. The two can pull apart in practice. A student might have very high self-efficacy for math specifically, feeling confident they can solve the problems in front of them, while still holding a fairly external locus of control overall, believing that grades in general depend more on a teacher's mood or luck on test day than on effort. Self-efficacy is task specific confidence in your own competence, while locus of control is a broader, more general belief about who or what tends to be in charge of outcomes.

Researchers have linked a more internal locus of control to a range of outcomes, including more proactive coping with stress, greater persistence after setbacks, and, in some studies, better academic performance and health related behavior, though these are correlational associations found across many studies rather than proof that an internal locus directly causes better outcomes for any given person. It also is not a strict either or category. Most people fall somewhere along a continuum rather than at a pure internal or pure external extreme, and a person's locus of control can shift somewhat depending on the specific domain of life in question, someone might feel quite internal about their career and quite external about their health, for example.

Locus of control is best understood as attribution theory's internal versus external dimension, but stretched out from a single moment to a general, fairly stable style of explaining life outcomes. That stability is exactly what makes it a personality trait rather than just a one time judgment, and it helps explain why some people respond to the same setback, a failed job interview, a breakup, a bad grade, by digging in and trying harder, while others respond by concluding that trying would not have mattered anyway.
